messages.subject_clean: getting 1d array from applying on 2d array, want 2d array at the end
messages.body_plain:
Hey Everyone,
I have a matrix where I need to apply a function that calculates the
frequency for columns 3-7, 8-12, 13-17, and 18-22, preserving the
first two columns.

myfunc<-function(x){a<-x[3:7]; c<-x[8:12]; g<-x[13:17];t<-x[18:22];
c(x{1:2],a/sum(a),c/sum(c),g/sum(g),t/sum(t)}
where a/sum(a) is a vector operation resulting in the fractional
vector

Here is a really short example of what this dataset looks like:
#Pos	Phred	A->A	A->C	A->G	A->T	A->N	C->A	C->C	C->G	C->T	C->N	G->A	G->C
G->G	G->T	G->N	T->A	T->C	T->G	T->T	T->N
0	2	8	1	2	2	3	1	3	2	2	0	1	1	3	1	2	18	14	22	23	2
0	11	28	1	1	5	0	2	14	2	1	0	1	1	20	1	0	13	8	18	42	0

I attempt to do the above operation on the above data structure row
wise with this:

result<-maply(data,1,myfunc)

Right now I am getting a 1d list out of the above operation! What I
want would be the same structure, but rather than counts, I want
fractions based on those sets of 5 elements like what I am attempting
in the above function.

First off I read in the data with the R function
read.table("filename.txt"), is maply the right function to use for
that datatype? Should I be changing the datatype or using a different
function?

A complete example of the data I am trying to do this on is here:
https://github.com/jstjohn/SimSeq/blob/master/examples/hiseq_mito_default_bwa_mapping_mq10_1.txt

Thanks everyone for your time and expertise on this! I currently have
the function written up and working nicely in python, but I would
really like to not have to rely on python to do this initial data
wrangling and produce an intermediate file when it seems like I can do
it all directly in R pretty easily.

messages.subject: Warning about incorrectly reordered output in aaply
messages.subject_clean: Warning about incorrectly reordered output in aaply
messages.body_plain:
Hi.  I have discovered a potentially critical bug in the aaply
functions (and maybe some of the other **ply functions) that you might
want to be aware of.  Hadley is aware of, and is fixing, this problem,
but he asked me to post what I found to the list.

The problem is with aaply reordering output in unexpected ways.  If
you have more than 10 items in a dimension, aaply has been permuting
the rows of output according to the character representation of the
row number (it's with columns, too).  So if you have, say, 12 rows
that you need to process, output row 1 corresponds to input row 1,
output row 2 corresponds to input row 10, output 3 to input 11, output
4 to input 12, output 5 to input 2, output 6 to input 3, and so
forth.  If you are expecting the output of a **ply function to
correspond to the order of the input, you really need to check that.
Where it was killing me was that the signs of regression coefficients
weren't making sense.  It was because the coefficient estimates were
matched to the wrong covariates.  Yikes!

There is a development version of plyr, 1.3, that I am now using (it's
up to Hadley if he wants to release that link to everyone).
Fortunately, the bug I described above is fixed in 1.3.   But there is
another bug that remains: re-ordering the output according to
dimnames.  If the row names are not in alphabetical order, the output
will be reordered so that the dimnames determine the order.  Unless
you are expecting that behavior, this kind of automated reordering can
cause a world of hurt.  For this, I have some test code (pasted below)
that illustrates the problem.  What I don't know is whether these
tests fail under 1.2.1, because I am now using 1.3, and I can't risk
going back.  If you are using 1.3, and maybe even 1.2.1, my
recommendation is that you remove ALL dimnames from any input arrays
to aaply.  Under 1.3, I think all of the problems disappear with that
workaround.  But if you are using 1.2.1, there may still be a problem
even without the dimnames.  In either case, if you are getting wacky
results from any of the **ply functions, this might be a reason why.

So here's the test code.  The W, V, and M tests pass in 1.3, but will
probably fail under 1.2.1 (again, I can't really test that).  The X,
Y, Z, P and Q tests should pass under 1.3, and would probably also
fail under 1.2.1.

X <-
array(1:12,dim=c(3,4),dimnames=list(R=LETTERS[c(13,12,14)],C=LETTERS[c(20,17,25,19)]))
X.1.right <- rowSums(X)
X.1.aaply <- aaply(X,1,sum)
cat("X: ",all.equal(X.1.right, X.1.aaply),"\n")

Y <-
array(1:60,dim=c(3,4,5),dimnames=list(R=c(13,12,14),C=c(20,17,25,19),L=c(1,3,5,2,4)))
Y.1.right <- colSums(Y,dim=2)
Y.1.aaply <- aaply(Y,3,sum)
cat("Y: ",all.equal(Y.1.right, Y.1.aaply),"\n")

Z <-
array(1:12,dim=c(3,4),dimnames=list(R=c(13,12,14),C=c(20,17,25,19)))
Z.1.right <- colSums(Z)
Z.1.aaply <- aaply(Z,2,sum)
cat("Z: ",all.equal(Z.1.right,Z.1.aaply),"\n")

W <- array(1:12,dim=c(3,4))
W.1.right <- colSums(W)
W.1.aaply <- aaply(W,2,sum)
cat("W: ",all.equal(W.1.right, W.1.aaply),"\n")

V <- array(1:(13*14),dim=c(13,14))
V.1.right <- colSums(V)
V.1.aaply <- aaply(V,2,sum)
cat("V: ",all.equal(V.1.right, V.1.aaply),"\n")

M <- array(1:(5*9*14),dim=c(5,9,14))
M.1.right <- colSums(M,dim=2)
M.1.aaply <- aaply(M,3,sum)
cat("M: ",all.equal(M.1.right, M.1.aaply),"\n")

P <- array(1:(5*9*14),dim=c(5,9,14),dimnames=list(A=1:5,B=1:9,C=14:1))
P.1.right <- colSums(P,dim=2)
P.1.aaply <- aaply(P,3,sum)
cat("P: ",all.equal(P.1.right, P.1.aaply),"\n")

Q <- array(1:(5*9*14),dim=c(5,9,14),dimnames=list(A=5:1,B=1:9,C=1:14))
Q.1.right <- colSums(Q,dim=2)
Q.1.aaply <- aaply(Q,3,sum)
cat("Q-dim3: ",all.equal(Q.1.right,Q.1.aaply),"\n")

Q.2.right <- rowSums(Q)
Q.2.aaply <- aaply(Q,1,sum)
cat("Q-rowSums: ",all.equal(Q.2.right,Q.2.aaply),"\n")

Michael Braun
MIT Sloan School of Management
bra...@mit.edu

messages.subject: Reshape discrepancy
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The following melt and two cast statements...

> datam<-melt(data,id=c("WID","SURV","Block","Year_2"))
> datac1<-cast(datam,WID~SURV,sum)
> datac2<-cast(datam,WID+Block+Year_2~SURV,sum)

...produce dataframes with these dimensions:

> dim(datac1)
[1] 3641    5
> dim(datac2)
[1] 3660    7

My intention with the second cast statement was simply to do exactly
the same thing as in the first cast statement, and to add two ID
columns (Block, Year_2) to the resulting dataframe. Indeed, datac2 had
two more columns (the correct ones) than datac1, but it also has more
rows.

Can anyone explain why the second dataframe (datac2) has more rows
than the first one (datac1)?

Also, what's the best way to compare two dataframes by producing a
third dataframe with the rows that aren't shared between them?

Many thanks for for your help,

Mark

messages.subject: max size for id (package plyr)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,

I am mostly a plyr newbie. Sorry if this question has been dealt with
before, couldn't find the answer on the mailing list or in the
documentation.

I was using ddply on a large dataset. I noticed that at a certain
size, I kept getting warning message about NAs. I played a bit more
with the code and did:

for (ind in 1:1000) {
a<-data.frame(x1=rnorm(200*ind), x2=rnorm(200*ind))
if (sum(is.na <http://is.na>(id(a)))>0) break()
}

It seems the code reliably breaks at iteration 232. Right now, it
looks to me like when I use the ddply call, it calls id (or
equivalent) on the variables that are used to split the data.frame,
and because those variables are too long, the numeric vector ends up
with NAs, and bad things happen.

Is the above correct? Is plyr (ddply) "safe" (in the sense of being
scaleable) for very large data.frames, sub-seted using multiple
variables? I am looking at a data.frame of a few million rows,
sub-seted using 3 column variables of the dataset. (I should have
enough RAM on the machine to compute that comfortably.)

I know I can get around this a few different ways for my particular
application, but it would be nice to know if there is some thing silly
I am missing that allows one to call ddply or id directly on a huge
dataframe.

Thanks!

Best,
Anirban

messages.subject_clean: Large data.frame with large number of grouping levels
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

As far as I can tell (and I am new to plyr so please do bear with me
if I am wrong), I think there is a "bug" in the sense that:

### START CODE

library(plyr)
rm(list=ls())

df <- data.frame (x1 = rep(1:1000,2), x2=rep(1:1000,2), x3=rep(1:500,4))
df$dat<-rnorm(nrow(df))
# works as expected
sumdat1 <- ddply(df, c("x1", "x2", "x3"), summarize, meandat = mean(dat))

nrow(sumdat1) # 1000
sumdat1[1,4] == (df$dat[1]+df$dat[1001])/2 # TRUE

# too big, does not work
df <- data.frame (x1 = rep(1:10000,2), x2=rep(1:10000,2), x3=rep(1:5000,4))
df$dat<-rnorm(nrow(df))
# warning message and wrong output
sumdat2 <- ddply(df, c("x1", "x2", "x3"), summarize, meandat = mean(dat))

# Warning message:
# In id(splits, drop = drop) : NAs introduced by coercion

nrow(sumdat2)  # I get 44 rows instead of 10000
sumdat2[1,4] == (df$dat[1]+df$dat[10001])/2 # TRUE (as expected)

### END CODE

Similarly if I do

### START CODE

for (ind in 1:1000) {
a<-data.frame(x1=rnorm(200*ind), x2=rnorm(200*ind))
if (sum(is.na <http://is.na>(id(a)))>0) break()
}

### breaks at iteration 232

### END CODE

Looks to me like when I use the ddply call, it calls id (or
equivalent) on the variables that are used to split the data.frame,
and because those variables are too long, the numeric vector ends up
with NAs, and bad things happen.

In case this is expected behavior, may I suggest some kind of warning
to the user that some row limit (and/or number of different "splits")
has been crossed. I know I spent a while trying to work out what was going on.

Thanks!

Best,
Anirban

On Sat, Dec 11, 2010 at 11:10 AM, Michael <bra...@mit.edu> wrote:
> Hi.  I have discovered a potentially critical bug in the aaply
> functions (and maybe some of the other **ply functions) that you might
> want to be aware of.  Hadley is aware of, and is fixing, this problem,
> but he asked me to post what I found to the list.
>
> The problem is with aaply reordering output in unexpected ways.  If
> you have more than 10 items in a dimension, aaply has been permuting
> the rows of output according to the character representation of the
> row number (it's with columns, too).  So if you have, say, 12 rows
> that you need to process, output row 1 corresponds to input row 1,
> output row 2 corresponds to input row 10, output 3 to input 11, output
> 4 to input 12, output 5 to input 2, output 6 to input 3, and so
> forth.  If you are expecting the output of a **ply function to
> correspond to the order of the input, you really need to check that.
> Where it was killing me was that the signs of regression coefficients
> weren't making sense.  It was because the coefficient estimates were
> matched to the wrong covariates.  Yikes!
>
> There is a development version of plyr, 1.3, that I am now using (it's
> up to Hadley if he wants to release that link to everyone).
> Fortunately, the bug I described above is fixed in 1.3.   But there is
> another bug that remains: re-ordering the output according to
> dimnames.  If the row names are not in alphabetical order, the output
> will be reordered so that the dimnames determine the order.  Unless
> you are expecting that behavior, this kind of automated reordering can
> cause a world of hurt.  For this, I have some test code (pasted below)
> that illustrates the problem.  What I don't know is whether these
> tests fail under 1.2.1, because I am now using 1.3, and I can't risk
> going back.  If you are using 1.3, and maybe even 1.2.1, my
> recommendation is that you remove ALL dimnames from any input arrays
> to aaply.  Under 1.3, I think all of the problems disappear with that
> workaround.  But if you are using 1.2.1, there may still be a problem
> even without the dimnames.  In either case, if you are getting wacky
> results from any of the **ply functions, this might be a reason why.
>
> So here's the test code.  The W, V, and M tests pass in 1.3, but will
> probably fail under 1.2.1 (again, I can't really test that).  The X,
> Y, Z, P and Q tests should pass under 1.3, and would probably also
> fail under 1.2.1.
>
> X <-
> array(1:12,dim=c(3,4),dimnames=list(R=LETTERS[c(13,12,14)],C=LETTERS[c(20,17,25,19)]))
> X.1.right <- rowSums(X)
> X.1.aaply <- aaply(X,1,sum)
> cat("X: ",all.equal(X.1.right, X.1.aaply),"\n")
>
> Y <-
> array(1:60,dim=c(3,4,5),dimnames=list(R=c(13,12,14),C=c(20,17,25,19),L=c(1,3,5,2,4)))
> Y.1.right <- colSums(Y,dim=2)
> Y.1.aaply <- aaply(Y,3,sum)
> cat("Y: ",all.equal(Y.1.right, Y.1.aaply),"\n")
>
> Z <-
> array(1:12,dim=c(3,4),dimnames=list(R=c(13,12,14),C=c(20,17,25,19)))
> Z.1.right <- colSums(Z)
> Z.1.aaply <- aaply(Z,2,sum)
> cat("Z: ",all.equal(Z.1.right,Z.1.aaply),"\n")
>
> W <- array(1:12,dim=c(3,4))
> W.1.right <- colSums(W)
> W.1.aaply <- aaply(W,2,sum)
> cat("W: ",all.equal(W.1.right, W.1.aaply),"\n")
>
> V <- array(1:(13*14),dim=c(13,14))
> V.1.right <- colSums(V)
> V.1.aaply <- aaply(V,2,sum)
> cat("V: ",all.equal(V.1.right, V.1.aaply),"\n")
>
> M <- array(1:(5*9*14),dim=c(5,9,14))
> M.1.right <- colSums(M,dim=2)
> M.1.aaply <- aaply(M,3,sum)
> cat("M: ",all.equal(M.1.right, M.1.aaply),"\n")
>
> P <- array(1:(5*9*14),dim=c(5,9,14),dimnames=list(A=1:5,B=1:9,C=14:1))
> P.1.right <- colSums(P,dim=2)
> P.1.aaply <- aaply(P,3,sum)
> cat("P: ",all.equal(P.1.right, P.1.aaply),"\n")
>
> Q <- array(1:(5*9*14),dim=c(5,9,14),dimnames=list(A=5:1,B=1:9,C=1:14))
> Q.1.right <- colSums(Q,dim=2)
> Q.1.aaply <- aaply(Q,3,sum)
> cat("Q-dim3: ",all.equal(Q.1.right,Q.1.aaply),"\n")
>
> Q.2.right <- rowSums(Q)
> Q.2.aaply <- aaply(Q,1,sum)
> cat("Q-rowSums: ",all.equal(Q.2.right,Q.2.aaply),"\n")
>
>
>
>
> Michael Braun
> MIT Sloan School of Management
> bra...@mit.edu
